findings.explanation: The sentence attributes 'other years' cohorts are similar' to 'the BLS note on this table', but the only BLS note in the document (line 665) explains the '_' and 'N' symbols; the similarity statement is this store's own verdict note, and the other cohorts' rows lie outside the cited lines.
findings.suggestion: Drop the attribution to a BLS note; if the comparison matters, add the adjacent cohorts' rows to the corpus through record-sources and cite them.

findings.explanation: The same BLS document's March 2013 cohort reads 34.7% in March 2023, exactly ten years on, so Shopify's sentence is accurate as written; 'although the cohort ... opened in 2015, not 2013' leaves a viewer thinking Shopify mixed up its cohort or matched by coincidence.
findings.suggestion: Remove the 'although ... not 2013' clause, or say only that the 2015 cohort we follow also ends its decade at 34.7 percent.

findings.explanation: The table counts private-sector establishments (single locations), not new businesses; the narration never says so, and 'most new businesses do close eventually' turns an establishment count into a business count, which the passage does not establish.
findings.suggestion: Say 'most new establishments in this table close eventually', and say once, early, that the table counts establishments (places of business), not companies.

findings.explanation: A rhetorical sentence that carries a factual comparison: Taylor's SBA figures (44% at four years, 31% at seven) sit well below the BLS cohort at the same ages (55.4% and 43.6%); the curve is not 'recognisably the same one', it is markedly steeper.
findings.suggestion: Say the second-hand figures agree that most close eventually, and that they show lower survival than the BLS cohort at four and seven years.

findings.explanation: 'Most within a few years: that part is not' ignores the script's own second source: Taylor's SBA figure has 56% of small businesses gone within four years, which is 'most within a few years'; only the BLS establishment cohort supports the verdict.
findings.suggestion: Scope the verdict to the BLS count ('in the government's establishment count, most are still open after three years') and acknowledge that the SBA figure Taylor cites is closer to the slogan.

findings.explanation: The writer's note admits it: the table carries no definition of an exit. That exits include sales and relocations rests only on the verdict note; no cited passage (or any line of the document) says so.
findings.suggestion: Cut the sentence, or add the BLS definitions page to the corpus through record-sources and cite its exact wording.

findings.explanation: A rhetorical sentence that smuggles facts: that a closure is an 'upper bound on failure' and that some closures were owners who sold up and left depend on the exit definition in s41, which no passage establishes.
findings.suggestion: Remove with s41, or keep only once a cited definition supports it.

findings.explanation: Set against 'the dramatic version' about e-commerce stores, an all-establishment one-year figure sounds like a refutation; the caveat that the table has no online-store breakdown arrives nine sentences later (s43).
findings.suggestion: Add 'though this table covers all establishments, not online stores' in this sentence.

findings.explanation: The passage does not say how the SBA counted, so 'independent' of the BLS table is not established, and 'points the same way' blurs that the SBA figures show noticeably lower survival.
findings.suggestion: Say 'A second set of numbers, quoted second-hand, ...' without 'independent', and frame the agreement as 'most close eventually'.

findings.explanation: Answers 'do most new businesses fail' with an establishment count and 'the government's own count' of closures, not of businesses or failures; the figures are right but the population and measure shift without saying so.
findings.suggestion: Say 'Not in the government's count of new establishments'.

findings.explanation: The figures are right, but 'the table shows why ... the survivors become harder to dislodge' reads a cause into a descriptive column (rising survival among survivors may be weak entrants leaving first), and 'each year' is not monotone (93.9 then 92.4).
findings.suggestion: Say 'the share of last year's survivors that make it through another year climbs from 79.6 to 86.8 to 88.9 percent'.

findings.explanation: 'Surviving the first year and the second ... is most of the game' implies most of the risk sits in the first two years; the cohort lost 30.9 points by March 2017 out of 65.3 over the decade, under half.
findings.suggestion: Say the first year carries the single largest loss, and drop 'most of the game'.

findings.explanation: 'the one the slogan usually reaches for' is a claim about how the slogan is quoted; of the four statements, only Barry's Economics uses five years (the others use months or ten years).

'every one of those closures was somebody's savings and somebody's plans' asserts that each closed establishment was an owner's own venture; the table counts establishments, which can be one location of a larger firm.
findings.suggestion: Say 'many of those closures were somebody's savings'.

findings.explanation: 'which sells the software many online stores run on' is a factual clause with no assertion; the post's context mentions sellers building on Shopify but nothing establishes 'many online stores'.
findings.suggestion: Say 'Shopify, the e-commerce platform, writes on its own blog ...'.

findings.explanation: 'An online shop can be opened in an afternoon for the price of a domain name' is a factual claim with no assertion or passage behind it.
findings.suggestion: Frame it as the videos' own pitch (Iman Gadzhi calls it 'very low upfront cost'), or cut it.

findings.explanation: The document's title is 'The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing', by Jon M. Taylor; 'The Case against MLM' is the store's short name, which a viewer searching for it may not find.

'Nowhere near the version we started with' sets the all-establishment first-year loss (20.4%) against The Plain Bagel's e-commerce figure with no caveat; s34 adds 'not online stores' to the same comparison, but fourteen sentences later. 'Many of those closures were somebody's savings' also reads closures as owners' ventures, which s58 says they need not be.
findings.suggestion: End at 'But it is not most', or add 'though that version was about online stores, which this table does not break out'.

findings.explanation: The quoted definition is the quarterly BED one; the age FAQ (L31) says the age and survival tables use the annual BED methodology, March to March, so for this table a closure is employment in one March and none the next. The substance (employment stopped, not why) is unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Optional: 'reported employment one March and none the next'.

findings.explanation: The linkage passage says unmatched records are matched on name, address and phone and forced by an analyst where possible, so a moved shop may be linked; 'nothing says' is still fair, since none of this settles relocations.
